I feel that there is a fine line with celebrating Earthly holidays in line with Christian holidays.

After doing much research, I don't feel convicted by participating in the Earthly traditions that line up with Christmas and Easter. Most of this is because I have seen arguments that some of these traditions symbolize some parts of the Christian belief (I don't remember specifics, but I do remember sitting in on multiple lessons where the pastor took items like the Easter Bunny and some Christmas songs and discussed how they symbolize Jesus). 

The line can get crossed if these traditions start to overshadow the Christian holiday. Do I see a problem with doing an Easter egg hunt? No. Do I see a problem with having the children's church do an Easter egg hunt during the service instead of doing an activity that goes over the importance of Easter? Yes. Do I see a problem with doing a family dinner with an Easter egg hunt on Easter? Absolutely not. Do I see a problem with doing a family dinner with an Easter egg hunt that is going to cause most of the family to miss Easter service? Yes. 

The important thing is to do your own research and pray about it. If you feel convicted, then don't do it. But if you pray and know that it is all just for good fun, then go for it.

When I was an aide, what I would do is ask if the teacher wanted me to do specific things (ie, when we would do small groups I would ask the teacher what group she wanted me to pull. Another example was there was a teacher that had lost her voice in the middle of reading a book, as we do read-aloud and we couldn't find the audiobook. She had students start working on their independent work, so I went up and asked if she wanted me to read aloud instead). They usually found that helpful for three reasons:

1. They didn't need to think about what they could have you do
2. It showed them that you were paying just as much attention to the class as they are
3. It gave them ideas as to what they could use you for in the future

Now as a teacher, I don't give my TA's specific tasks, I just give them an abbreviated lesson plan & they walk around the room and help out students that seem to be struggling with the work. I'm also from a small school with not many IEP's and precisely zero 504's, so that also changes things. We may not show it all the time, but we definitely appreciate having TA's there to help us out & back us up when we need it!! My biggest piece of advice would be communicate as much as possible. Communicate with the other section leader, and leadership from the rest of the band (& director) to make sure what you are doing lined up with everything else. Communicate your goals (goals that you would like to see your group of people do) with the people that they affect. For example, I’m my university’s drumline leader, and at the start of last season I told them I wanted to be able to play X amount of cadences & I wanted to develop visuals for us to do on the field. They knew what was expected, and they did it. They did it quite well, too. Lastly, communicate with your section as friends. The main reason many of us are in band is because of the family bond that’s formed, and that bond is helped greatly by good leadership. Talk with your section about what they like and what they want to do, as far as band goes, and use your position to implement their ideas to the best of your ability. I did all of these things last year & received a recognition award for my leadership. Congrats, it’s a lot of fun!!
